`git rebase --onto` lets you choose a new base for a range of commits. Plain `git rebase` always replays your commits onto the branch you name. With `--onto` you also choose which commits get moved.

## Syntax

```
git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> [<branch>]
```

Git takes the commits that are on `<branch>` but not on `<upstream>`, i.e. the range `<upstream>..<branch>`, and replays them on top of `<newbase>`. If you leave out `<branch>`, it uses the current branch.

## Example: move a branch off another feature branch

You started `feature-b` from `feature-a`, but `feature-b` should really be based on `main`:

```
main:       A---B
                 \
feature-a:        C---D
                       \
feature-b:              E---F
```

`feature-b` contains C and D (from `feature-a`) as well as its own commits E and F. To move only E and F onto `main`:

```bash
git rebase --onto main feature-a feature-b
```

This means: "take the commits on `feature-b` that aren't in `feature-a` (E and F) and replay them onto `main`."

Result:

```
main:       A---B
                |\
feature-a:      | C---D
                 \
feature-b:        E'---F'
```

E' and F' are new commits with the same changes as E and F but new hashes. C and D stay on `feature-a` and aren't part of `feature-b` anymore.

## Other common uses

- **Delete commits from the middle of a branch.** To drop commits D and E from `A-B-C-D-E-F`, run `git rebase --onto C E`. This replays F directly onto C.
- **Recover after an upstream rewrite.** If the branch you built on was rebased or squashed, run `--onto` with the new upstream as `<newbase>` and the old upstream commit as `<upstream>`. Only your own commits get moved.

## Tips

- Run `git log --oneline <upstream>..<branch>` first to see exactly which commits will move.
- Rebasing creates new commit hashes. Avoid rebasing branches other people have already pulled, unless everyone involved agrees.
- If something goes wrong, `git rebase --abort` cancels a rebase that's still in progress. After a rebase has finished, `git reflog` shows the old commit hashes so you can reset back to them.
